prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, which opened a new regime of precision in time and frequency measurement

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks first. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the trapping-light shift, so many atoms can be interrogated at once, and that is what turned a clever concept into an instrument. The instrument was then taken, experimentally and in several independent laboratories, to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, to millimetre-scale gravitational redshift measurements, and to a credible route toward redefining the second. Seven of eight openings ranked it, which I read as a sign of breadth and not of weak support, and no colleague's ballot contests the credited pair. The attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: Katori for the proposal and first strontium lattice clock, Ye for the systematic-uncertainty and stability records and the many-body clock work. It also has the property I weigh most as an experimentalist, which is that it changes what can be measured and so opens observations (geodesy, constants, dark-matter searches) that were not available before.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this could be read as an evolution of a metrology lineage that already has prizes (Hall and Hansch 2005 for the comb, Wineland and Haroche 2012 for control of single quantum systems, ion clocks included), and as a technical advance more than a new physical effect. A second point is that the second has not been redefined yet and the ion-clock and nuclear-clock communities have competing claims on what the best clock is. Third, I rank this from memory on the precise uncertainty figures and on who first articulated the magic-wavelength idea; I have not checked those against the record. Finally, a two-person prize leaves out the Sr/Yb community around Lemonde, Takamoto and others, which a careful citation must handle.

responses.point: Eva Lindroth also ranks lattice clocks first and stresses that the Hall and Wineland prizes partly overlap in the clock lineage, so the committee must show the new content is distinct, and that the magic-wavelength attribution was discussed in parallel by other groups.
responses.response: I agree with both the support and the qualification. The distinct content is the magic-wavelength condition: the Hall and Hansch prize gave us the comb as a ruler, and the 2012 prize gave control of single trapped quantum systems, but neither made it possible to interrogate a large ensemble without trapping-light shifts, which is what gives the stability and the 1e-18 systematics. I would draft the citation around the lattice scheme and its realisation rather than around clocks in general, to keep that separation visible. On parallel proposals, I think the record supports Katori as the person who proposed and demonstrated, but I would like the committee's own check on priority before finalising.

responses.point: Bernhard Mehlig ranks the clocks only eighth and worries that a clock prize sits close to the 2005 and 2012 prizes and that competing approaches (ions, the thorium nuclear clock) bear on timing; his own first choice is Kardar-Parisi-Zhang universality.
responses.response: The overlap concern is fair and I take it seriously, but I would separate subject adjacency from content overlap. Time metrology is the subject of all three prizes; what was recognised is different each time. The ion and nuclear clocks are not an argument to wait, since the lattice clocks are the ones that have been independently reproduced and surpassed by NIST, RIKEN, PTB, SYRTE and others for over a decade, whereas the thorium clock is a demonstration stage. I would also ask Bernhard to say what the discovery in B056 is that is independent of the 1986 theory, since the experimental confirmation by Takeuchi is the part I would want to see tested for reproducibility, and the exact-solution authors are outside the credited names.

responses.point: Eva Olsson ranks the clocks fourth, finds the pair a good fit, and raises whether single-ion clocks and the Al+ work by Wineland and Rosenband make the field attribution broader than the credited pair, and whether the split between proposal and precision realisation is right.
responses.response: The Al+ clock is an excellent instrument, but it is a different route, and it leans on the quantum-logic spectroscopy that was part of the 2012 recognition, so I do not think it enters the lattice-clock credit. The proposal and realisation split is the reason I want both Katori and Ye: one without the other would credit either an unproven idea or a record without its origin. I do not think this requires a third name, though I accept that Lemonde and Takamoto will be mentioned in the scientific background. Her main alternative, magic-angle graphene, is attractive, but I would give more weight than she does to the open pairing mechanism and to the omission of the first experimental author, which make attribution harder there than for clocks.

responses.point: Ulf Danielsson puts the ATLAS and CMS Higgs discovery first as an overdue discovery-first case with a defensible three-person configuration of project leaders, and ranks lattice clocks third, noting that Ye also appears in a nuclear-clock candidate.
responses.response: I agree the Higgs observation is of the highest importance and extremely mature, and I do not rank it highly only because of the attribution problem that Eva Olsson and Mark Pearce also identify: spokespersons and founders are not necessarily those who made the decisive measurement, and I cannot evaluate that from the record. That is a practical difficulty, not a verdict on merit. On Ye and the nuclear clock, I do not see a complication: the lattice-clock work is a finished, independently reproduced achievement, and any later nuclear-clock recognition would be a different citation. I am glad he already supports exactly the Katori and Ye pair.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges optical lattice clocks as a distinct discovery or as the continuation of the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes.
Whether to wait for the formal redefinition of the second, or for stronger evidence in the nuclear-clock work.
Priority of the magic-wavelength proposal relative to parallel proposals, which I have not verified.
Which of Cirac-Zoller-Blatt or Bloch-Greiner-Esslinger is the better fallback, given the Zoller overlap and the 2012 prize.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict that requires recusal is apparent. For transparency: I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory at JILA during my PhD, and Jun Ye works in that environment, so I have a loose scientific acquaintance with the community, but I have no collaboration with Katori or Ye that I can identify from my profile. My Lund and WACQT affiliations are relevant mainly to B017 and the quantum-information candidates, not to B002.
